summary: Describes the syslog protocol used to carry event notification messages. It uses a layered design that allows different transports, and defines a message format with structured vendor extensions. This is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 3164.

eli5.summary: Computers keep a diary of events, and syslog is the way they send diary entries to a central notebook. It defines the shape of each entry.

questions: what is the syslog message format
how is the syslog priority value calculated
what is structured data in syslog
subtitle: A standard, transport-independent format for the event messages that devices and programs send to a log collector.

tldr.problem: Syslog was widely used but never formally standardized, and each new reliable or secure syslog extension would have had to invent its own packet format and transport.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5424 separates message content from transport. It defines one message format (a header, optional structured data and a free-form text) and leaves delivery to transport mappings, with TLS required and UDP recommended.
tldr.outcome: It is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes the Informational RFC 3164, giving syslog extensions a common foundation to build on.

today: RFC 5424 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2009 and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It obsoletes RFC 3164.

sections.title: Why Syslog Needed a Standard
sections.content:
RFC 5424 describes the syslog protocol, which is used to convey event notification messages. Its goal is a layered architecture that separates message content from message transport, while keeping each layer easy to extend.

The RFC explains why this was needed. Standardization efforts for reliable and secure syslog extensions lacked a Standards-Track, transport-independent RFC. Without one, every extension would define its own packet format and transport, and subtle compatibility problems would build up over time. Written once at the message layer, code can then serve every transport.

The document does not describe how messages are stored. It calls storage out of scope and unnecessary for interoperability. It obsoletes RFC 3164, an Informational document that described implementations found in the field.
sections.eli5: Before this, every tool wrote its diary entries a little differently. This document is the rule book so that everyone writes them the same way, no matter how the mail is delivered.

sections.title: Layers and Roles
sections.content:
Syslog uses three layers. Syslog content is the management information inside a message. The syslog application layer generates, interprets, routes and stores messages. The syslog transport layer puts messages on the wire and takes them off.

Three roles live at the application layer. An originator generates syslog content. A collector gathers content for further analysis. A relay accepts messages from originators or other relays and forwards them to collectors or other relays. A transport sender and a transport receiver hand messages to and from a specific transport protocol.

The basic principles are short. Syslog does not acknowledge delivery, so conceptually it is a pure simplex protocol. Originators and relays may be configured to send the same message to several collectors and relays. Originator, relay and collector functions may all reside on one system.
sections.eli5: One computer writes the note, maybe a few helpers pass it along, and one computer files it. Nobody writes back to say the note arrived.

sections.title: Transport Mappings
sections.content:
RFC 5424 specifies no transport. It only describes the message format in a transport-independent way and leaves transports to other documents. All implementations MUST support a TLS-based transport as described in RFC 5425. They SHOULD also support a UDP-based transport as described in RFC 5426, which stays consistent with the traditional UDP use. Deployments are RECOMMENDED to use TLS.

A transport MUST NOT deliberately alter the message. Any temporary change made at the sender must be reversed at the receiver, so the relay or collector sees an exact copy. Otherwise end-to-end cryptographic verifiers such as signatures would break.

Message size limits come from the transport mapping. Every transport receiver MUST accept messages of up to and including 480 octets, and SHOULD accept up to 2048 octets. A receiver that gets something larger than it supports SHOULD truncate the payload, or MAY discard the message. Truncation must happen at the end of the message.
sections.eli5: The rule book does not say which postal service to use, only that the letter must arrive unchanged. It does say every mailbox has to be able to take a small letter.

sections.title: The Message and Its Header
sections.content:
A syslog message is a HEADER, a space, the STRUCTURED-DATA, and optionally a space and a free-form MSG. The header has seven parts, separated by spaces: PRI and VERSION (joined), TIMESTAMP, HOSTNAME, APP-NAME, PROCID and MSGID. The header is seven-bit ASCII. A field with nothing to say uses the NILVALUE, a single hyphen.

PRI is a number in angle brackets that combines Facility and Severity. The Priority value is the Facility times 8 plus the Severity. A local use 4 message (Facility 20) with Severity 5 (Notice) is <165>. Facility MUST be 0 to 23 and Severity 0 to 7, and leading zeros are not allowed except for the value 0 itself. The tables of facilities and severities are informational.

VERSION is 1 in this document and MUST be incremented for any new specification that changes the header. TIMESTAMP is derived from RFC 3339 with stricter rules: the T is required, T and Z must be upper case, leap seconds MUST NOT be used, and fractional seconds have at most 6 digits. A device that cannot get the time MUST send the NILVALUE.

HOSTNAME should be the fully qualified domain name, falling back in order to a static IP address, a hostname, a dynamic IP address and finally the NILVALUE. APP-NAME and MSGID are strings meant for filtering at a relay or collector, such as a firewall using the MSGID TCPIN for incoming TCP traffic. PROCID has no interoperable meaning except that a change in its value signals a discontinuity in syslog reporting.
sections.eli5: Each entry starts with a label: how urgent it is, when it happened, which computer wrote it, which program, and what kind of event. A dash means I do not know.

sections.title: Structured Data and SD-IDs
sections.content:
STRUCTURED-DATA carries information in an easily parseable form, for example meta-information about the message or application data such as traffic counters. It holds zero or more SD-ELEMENTs, and with zero elements it MUST contain the NILVALUE. Each element is written in square brackets as an SD-ID followed by name="value" parameters, for example [exampleSDID@32473 iut="3" eventSource="Application" eventID="1011"].

There are two kinds of SD-ID. Names without an at-sign are assigned by IETF Review and must be registered with IANA. Anyone can define others in the form name@<private enterprise number>, such as ourSDID@32473. The same SD-ID MUST NOT appear twice in a message. Parameter values are UTF-8 and the characters ", \ and ] MUST be escaped with a backslash. Elements sit directly next to each other, so a space between two elements ends the structured data. Once defined, an SD-ID or parameter name MUST NOT change meaning; a new one must be created instead.

The RFC defines three optional SD-IDs. timeQuality describes how far to trust the timestamp (tzKnown, isSynced, syncAccuracy). origin identifies the sender (ip, enterpriseId, software, swVersion). meta carries sequenceId, sysUpTime and language. The sequenceId starts at 1 and wraps back to 1 after 2147483647.

The free-form MSG SHOULD be Unicode in UTF-8. If it is UTF-8, it MUST start with the byte order mark and use the shortest form. Syslog applications SHOULD avoid octets below 32 and MAY modify them on receipt.
sections.eli5: Besides the plain-English note, an entry can carry a tidy form with labeled boxes, like name: value, that a computer can read without guessing. Companies can add their own boxes using their own number so they never clash.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC lists many risks. Syslog has no replay detection: an attacker can record normal-looking messages and send them later, even adjusting the timestamp, and signing messages would stop that. Reliable delivery is not described, so messages can be lost to congestion or be deliberately discarded to hide activity. There is no confidentiality in the format itself, so a secure transport mapping is advised.

Unicode and control characters are a second family of problems. An attacker may hide information after a NUL character, use backspace characters to make part of a log unreadable, or inject control characters through invalid UTF-8. Requiring the shortest form for UTF-8 guards against the technical issues, though visual spoofing remains.

Truncation can also be abused, so important information should come early in the message. Finally, the RFC warns about congestion on UDP (which lacks congestion control, one reason TLS is required), forwarding loops between misconfigured relays, collectors whose disks are filled with false messages, and denial of service in general. If messages must be dropped, it RECOMMENDS dropping lower severity first.
sections.eli5: A sneaky person could resend old diary pages, hide a page, or peek at them on the way. The rule book tells you to use a sealed envelope and to keep the important news at the top.

sections.title: Relationship to BSD Syslog
sections.content:
The appendix explains that BSD syslog was in widespread use but never formally standardized. RFC 3164 described observed formats, and the research for RFC 5424 found very little in common between implementations. The only thing they all agree on is that a message starts with <PRIVAL>, so RFC 5424 keeps the PRI syntax and meaning, which lets legacy systems file new messages correctly.

The newer format is easier to parse. The old TAG is split into APP-NAME, PROCID and MSGID, and what RFC 3164 called CONTENT is now MSG. The old timestamp had less precision and no year or time zone. RFC 5424 does not specify relay behavior, which it says might be covered elsewhere. The appendix is helpful guidance and is not required for compliance.
sections.eli5: The old way of writing entries was a bit of a free-for-all. The new way keeps the one thing everybody already did the same, and tidies the rest.
